title: The Sum and Product Rules
short: Add the counts of cases that cannot happen together; multiply the counts of choices made one after another.
trouble: Students multiply when the cases are alternatives (either/or) that should be added, or add when the choices are made in sequence.

blocks.html: In probability you counted permutations by multiplying choices. That multiplication is one of two basic rules of counting. Both rules are facts about sets you have seen: the size of a union of separate sets, and the size of a Cartesian product.

Sum rule: if a choice can be made in one of several ways that cannot happen together, with $a$, $b$, … options in each, the total is $a + b + \cdots$. Product rule: if a choice is made in steps, with $a$ options for the first step and $b$ for the second (whatever the first was), and so on, the total is $a \cdot b \cdots$.

The sum rule is $|A \cup B| = |A| + |B|$ for disjoint sets: nothing is counted twice because nothing is in both. The product rule is $|A \times B| = |A| \cdot |B|$: a two-step choice is an ordered pair, and each first step pairs with every second step. The words to listen for: "either … or" (alternatives, add) versus "first … then" (a sequence, multiply). Big problems often need both: split into cases with the sum rule, count each case with the product rule.

blocks.title: A license plate
blocks.q: A plate has $3$ letters (A–Z) followed by $3$ digits (0–9), repeats allowed. How many plates are there?
steps: Six steps in a row: $26$ choices for each letter and $10$ for each digit.

blocks.title: Two possible lengths
blocks.q: A code uses digits 0–9 and has length $3$ or $4$. How many codes are there?
steps: A code has one length or the other, never both, so split into cases and add.

blocks.title: Cases, then products
blocks.q: How many three-digit numbers are even and have three different digits?
steps: The last digit must be even, and $0$ behaves differently because the first digit cannot be $0$. So split by the last digit.
Last digit $0$: first digit $1$–$9$ ($9$ ways), middle digit anything else ($8$ ways): $9 \cdot 8 = 72$.
Last digit $2$, $4$, $6$ or $8$ ($4$ ways): first digit not $0$ and not the last digit ($8$ ways), middle digit not either of those ($8$ ways): $4 \cdot 8 \cdot 8 = 256$.

blocks.html: Multiplying alternatives or adding a sequence. "Choose a dessert: one of $4$ pies or one of $3$ cakes" is $4 + 3 = 7$, not $12$; there is no second step. "Choose a pie and a cake" is $4 \cdot 3 = 12$, not $7$. Check: ask whether one outcome involves both choices (multiply) or just one of them (add).
